Following yolk absorption and mouth opening, the free-swimming larva enters a pelagic phase characterized by rapid somatic growth. Growth trajectories derived from scale annuli indicate that puberty is attained at a body length of 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters], a relatively modest size compared to other members of the genus.

At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals of Notropis potteri have a corresponding wet weight of approximately 0.72 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.72 grams]. This value represents a considerable multiple of the hatching mass, reflecting the substantial investment in somatic growth that precedes reproductive maturation. Comparative analysis with congeneric species such as Notropis longirostris and Notropis texanus indicates that the pubertal length of 4.5 cm [Lp = 4.5 cm] is near the lower end of the range observed for the genus, suggesting a relatively early maturation schedule. This early onset of reproduction may be an adaptive response to the variable flow regimes and unpredictable habitat availability characteristic of the species’ prairie stream environment.

This maximum reproductive rate, recorded from individuals measuring 4.9 centimeters in total length, demonstrates the species’ capacity for sustained, iteroparous reproduction. The daily rate is relatively modest when compared to other cyprinids of similar body size, likely reflecting constraints imposed by the limited abdominal cavity volume available for ovarian development. Spawning events are thought to be multiple and protracted across the late spring and summer months. The thermal regime of 20 °C is near the optimal temperature for both gonadal recrudescence and larval survival in this species, and deviations from this temperature have been shown to reduce clutch output significantly in related taxa.

Individuals that delay reproduction risk never contributing to the next generation if an episodic disturbance such as a flood or drought eliminates the local population. As a consequence, selection has likely favored the early allocation of resources to gamete production even at the expense of continued somatic growth.
